paper.title: Long-term relatedness and income distribution: understanding the deep roots of inequality
paper.code_data_availability: Supplementary material is available on the OUP website. It contains data, replication code, and an Online Appendix (p. 724). No Statistics Denmark (DST) project reference is given; the paper uses no Danish administrative register.

registers.role: outcomes (Gini of disposable income; also Gini of market income for the aRedist and rRedist mediators)

registers.name_in_paper: Genetic distance data of Spolaore and Wacziarg (2009), built on Cavalli-Sforza et al. (1994)
World Bank Poverty and Inequality Platform

registers.role: individual-level outcome and controls for the mechanism analysis

registers.name_in_paper: Ancestry-adjusted genetic diversity index (Ashraf and Galor, 2013)
Worldwide Governance Indicators (average of six dimensions, called Institutions)
Fractionalization (Alesina et al., 2003) and Polarization (Desmet et al., 2012)

linkages: Countries linked to their genetic distance to Denmark via the Cavalli-Sforza et al. (1994) ancestral-population matching used by Spolaore and Wacziarg (2009)
Country pairs formed from every ordered pair i != j of countries with a Gini observation and a pairwise genetic distance
European Social Survey respondents linked to their parents' country of origin, and through it to that country's Gdist_DNK and geographic characteristics

sample.universe: Countries of the world with available data on disposable income inequality and genetic distance (up to 118 countries); and, for the mechanism analysis, second-generation Europeans in the European Social Survey
sample.unit_of_observation: Country (cross-section); country pair (Table 5); individual survey respondent (Table 6)
selection_rules: Keep countries with a non-missing SWIID Gini averaged over 2000-2015 and a non-missing Gdist_DNK: 118 countries
IV specifications additionally require Gdist_1500: 116 countries
Adding 'proximate' controls reduces the sample to between 101 and 118 countries
Adding fundamental controls reduces the sample to between 66 and 118 countries (Individualism 83, Social trust 75, all ten simultaneously 66)
Bilateral analysis: all ordered country pairs i != j with non-missing Gini and pairwise genetic distance (9,423 pairs; 7,358 and 6,763 with controls)
Fixed-effects filtered estimator: 104 countries with panel data, 1990-2015

Individual-level analysis: EU-born respondents whose parents are foreign-born, split into those whose parents are from the same foreign country (20,728), whose father is foreign (30,661) and whose mother is foreign (29,778)
sample.period: Gini averaged 2000-2015; annual series 1990-2015 (Gini) and 1980-2021 (top 10% income share); European Social Survey 2002-2020
sample.n_individuals: 20,728 / 30,661 / 29,778 second-generation European respondents in the three Table 6 samples

construction_notes: Gdist_DNK is the LOG of Nei's (1972) genetic distance to Denmark; Denmark is chosen as the base country because it is the world frontier of egalitarian income distribution (Gini of 24.05 between 2000 and 2015 in Solt's data).
Only neutral genes, whose changes are random and independent of selection pressure, enter the genetic distance index.
Gini is averaged between 2000 and 2015 before estimating the cross-sectional models.

Region dummies: East Asia and Pacific, Europe and Central Asia, Latin America and Caribbean, Middle East and North Africa, North America, South Asia; sub-Saharan Africa is excluded as the base category.

Bilateral controls are absolute differences in the country-level geographic variables, plus geographic proximity and a contiguity dummy; 21 pairwise regional dummies equal one if two countries do not belong to a pairwise region.
aRedist = Gini_market - Gini_net; rRedist = (Gini_market - Gini_net) / Gini_market.

Table 1 descriptive statistics (N = 118): Gini mean 0.394, SD 0.082, min 0.239, max 0.655; Gdist_DNK mean 4.324, SD 1.266, min 1.081, max 5.772; Gdist_1500 (N = 116) mean 6.175, SD 1.905, min 0.000, max 7.735.
This is NOT a Danish-register study: Denmark enters only as the reference country of the genetic-distance measure. No DST register or register variable is used.

claims.statement: Greater log genetic distance to Denmark raises the Gini coefficient of post-tax, post-transfer disposable household income across countries (OLS; without world-region dummies).

definition.value: Log of genetic distance to Denmark. Genetic distance is Nei's (1972) measure built from the 'expected heterozygosity' index of allele frequencies of neutral genes (Cavalli-Sforza et al., 1994; Spolaore and Wacziarg, 2009); it proxies the length of time elapsed since two populations separated from a common ancestor. Denmark is the base country because it is the world frontier of egalitarian income distribution.

timing.value: Time-invariant, deep-rooted (ancestral separation measured over the prehistoric and historic past); one value per country

definition.value: Gini coefficient of inequality of post-tax, post-transfer (disposable) household income, taken from the Standardized World Income Inequality Database (SWIID) (Solt, 2020). Data on Gini are averaged between 2000 and 2015 to estimate the cross-sectional models.

timing.value: Country average over 2000-2015

units.value: Gini points on the 0-1 scale (Table 1: Gini mean 0.394, min 0.239, max 0.655) per one-unit increase in log genetic distance to Denmark

estimand.formal_query: E[Gini | do(Gdist_DNK = g+1)] - E[Gini | do(Gdist_DNK = g)] for countries worldwide

population.description: Cross-section of up to 118 countries worldwide with non-missing data on the Gini coefficient of disposable income inequality and log genetic distance to Denmark
population.selection: Countries are included only where both the SWIID Gini (averaged 2000-2015) and the genetic distance measures are available; IV columns additionally require Gdist_1500, which drops the sample to 116.

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-country (or country-pair) variation in deep-rooted genetic distance, a proxy for the time elapsed since two populations separated from a common ancestor

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional ignorability: given the geographic/agroclimatic controls and world-region dummies, Gdist_DNK is as good as randomly assigned with respect to the unobserved determinants of income inequality.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper motivates the control set as addressing omitted variable bias and shows the coefficient is insensitive to adding geographic controls and region dummies (Table 2, cols 1-2), the 'proximate' causes (Table 3) and the fundamental causes (Table 4).

key_assumptions.assumption: No reverse causation: contemporary income inequality does not cause deep-rooted genetic distance.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from the deep-rooted, predetermined nature of genetic distance rather than tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Units are independent: one country's genetic distance to Denmark does not affect another country's income inequality (no interference across countries), despite the mechanism being cross-border policy diffusion.

definition.value: Log of genetic distance to Denmark. Genetic distance is Nei's (1972) measure built from the 'expected heterozygosity' index of allele frequencies of neutral genes (Cavalli-Sforza et al., 1994; Spolaore and Wacziarg, 2009); it proxies the length of time elapsed since two populations separated from a common ancestor. Denmark is the base country because it is the world frontier of egalitarian income distribution.
